On the tenth night the sea threw him up on the island of Calypso.
She was a nymph, a goddess, beautiful, and she lived alone in a cave hung with vines and surrounded by springs.
She saved his life, and fed him, and fell in love with him.
And she wouldn't let him leave.
He was there for seven years.
Stay with me, she said, and I'll make you immortal.
You'll never get old, and you'll never die.
And every day Odysseus went down to the beach, sat on the rocks, looked out at the sea, and cried.
All he wanted was to see the smoke rising from Ithaca one more time, and then he was happy to die.
He turned down living forever so he could go back to a small rocky island and a wife who was getting older without him.
I've always liked him most here.
In the end the gods took pity on him.
Poseidon was away at a feast at the far end of the world.
And while he was gone, Athena, goddess of wisdom, who'd always had a soft spot for Odysseus because he was so clever, went to Zeus.
Zeus sent Hermes to Calypso with an order to let him go.
You gods can't stand it, she said, when a goddess loves a mortal man.
But she did as she was told.
She gave him tools, and he cut down trees and built a raft with his own hands.
On the eighteenth day at sea he saw land.
And Poseidon, coming home from his feast, saw him.
He gathered up every cloud in the sky and stirred the sea with his trident, and the raft came apart.
For two days and two nights Odysseus swam.
On the third day, more dead than alive, he dragged himself up the mouth of a river onto a beach.
He buried himself in a pile of dry leaves, and slept.
He woke up to the sound of girls playing ball.
A princess named Nausicaa had come down to the river with her maids to wash clothes.
Then a naked man, crusted with salt, stepped out of the bushes holding a leafy branch in front of himself.
She gave him clothes and brought him to her father, king of the Phaeacians, who were the finest sailors in the world.
At the feast that night a blind singer picked up his lyre and sang about the Trojan War.
He sang about the wooden horse, and about the clever man who'd thought of it.
The stranger at the table pulled his cloak over his face and wept.
The king asked him, gently, who he was.
For the first time since the Cyclops, he said his name out loud.
Then he told them everything that had happened since Troy, ending with the cattle of the Sun, and the name of every man he'd lost along the way.
The Phaeacians sat listening, in silence, until midnight.
The next evening they put him on one of their ships, loaded with gifts.
And he fell into a sleep so deep it was almost like death, while the ship skimmed over the water faster than a hawk.
When he woke up, he was lying on a beach he didn't recognise.
He'd come home late, and alone, on somebody else's ship, just as the Cyclops had prayed.
